tool.name: Chelsea filter
tool.measures: the reaction of a stone to a filter that only lets through yellow-green and deep red
tool.where: Gemmology House and Office, bottom row, in the middle of the laboratory (a lamp is placed underneath)
tips: Stone on white paper, strong tungsten light
Hold the filter close to your eye

steps.title: A filter with two windows
steps.text: A coloured stone lets part of the light through: it can be analysed with filters. The most important is the Chelsea filter, a small coloured filter that stops almost the whole spectrum. It only lets two windows through: yellow-green and deep red. A stone that sends back a lot of deep red therefore looks red through it.

steps.title: Chromium turns red
steps.text: Chromium makes deep red glow: ruby, alexandrite and emerald look red, or pink, through the filter. Cobalt also turns red (synthetic spinel, blue glass). Iron does not: a stone coloured by iron stays greenish or greyish. The filter helps separate stones of the same colour in a lot, spot an intruder in a piece of jewellery or a necklace, and detect a treated, assembled or synthetic stone.

steps.title: Using the filter
steps.text: 1. Place the stone on a sheet of white paper. 2. Light it with a strong tungsten source: in the laboratory, switch on the lamp. 3. Hold the filter close to your eye and look at the stone through it. 4. Note the colour, and compare with a reference stone. The darker the colour of the stone, the harder the reaction is to see.

steps.title: What it shows
steps.text: • Ruby, natural or synthetic: red to very bright red. • Emerald: bright red or pink to greenish. • Alexandrite, demantoid: pink to bright red. • Synthetic blue spinel (cobalt): bright red, orange-pink or pink. Natural blue spinel: reddish to greyish green. • Blue sapphire: generally dark green. • Almandine garnet: greyish to dark red. • Red glass: dark red; cobalt blue: intense red to pink.

steps.title: Cobalt blue spinel or sapphire?
steps.text: Two blue stones, almost identical to the naked eye: a synthetic blue spinel, coloured by cobalt, and a blue sapphire, coloured by iron. Through the filter: • the cobalt spinel turns red: bright red, orange-pink or pink; • the sapphire stays dark green. Cobalt, like chromium, lets deep red through; iron does not. Natural blue spinel is reddish to greyish green: the filter alone is not enough, it is cross-checked with the spectroscope (three cobalt bands) and the index.

steps.title: Caution
steps.text: Results vary with the intensity of the colour, and with the relative concentration of the colouring elements when there are several. A reaction to the filter is never a diagnostic result: it is an indication. The test is quick and easy, but results must be interpreted with caution, because new varieties of stones, natural or synthetic, may react differently from the table.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text:
• The filter only lets through yellow-green and deep red.
• Chromium turns red under the filter, and so does cobalt; iron does not.
• You need a strong tungsten source, the stone on white paper, the filter close to the eye.
• An indication, never an identification: it is combined with the spectroscope, the index and the density.
